dbarts as a Component

Vincent Dorie

2026-08-15

Source: vignettes/dbarts-as-a-component.Rmd
dbarts-as-a-component.Rmd

A dbartsSampler is a mutable object that runs one sweep at a time, so BART can be a conditional model inside a larger Gibbs or Metropolis-Hastings scheme rather than the whole of it. Seven recipes follow. The first six are complete, runnable outer samplers; each answers the same three questions, which are the ones a composition gets wrong:

  • which channel the outer block writes – response, offset, weights, sigma, or a predictor column;
  • which fit the outer block reads back, since the six reporting methods do not report the same quantity (?dbartsSampler, “Reading the fit”);
  • whose prior is in force, since a swapped response does not re-anchor the leaf prior the sampler was built with.

?dbarts-embedding is the reference page for the channels and the reads; this vignette is the worked set. Recipes 1 through 6 are each also a cell in the package’s test suite, because a composition that runs to completion can still be sampling the wrong posterior. The seventh recipe is different in kind: it drives bart() itself through a compiled per-draw callback rather than a dbartsSampler loop, and is not evaluated here – it needs a C++ compiler dbarts does not depend on – so its own check is a plain-C copy of the same callback under inst/tinytest, not a chunk in this file.

Throughout, run(0L, 1L) advances the sampler exactly one sweep, and every recipe builds its sampler the same way:

n <- 200L
nBurn <- 100L
nDraws <- 100L

# a single seeded chain that serializes no state on a per-sweep mutation
recipeControl <- function(seed) {
  dbartsControl(n.chains = 1L, n.threads = 1L, n.trees = 25L,
                updateState = FALSE, seed = seed)
}

1. Data augmentation written in R

A binary response is fit by drawing a per-observation latent and regressing on it. dbarts will do this internally with family = "probit", but a host that needs the latent for its own blocks – a selection equation, a shared factor – can run the Albert-Chib step itself with dbartsDrawLatents and dbartsWorkingResponse over an ordinary gaussian sampler.

Two details make it correct rather than merely runnable. The sampler’s residual standard deviation is pinned at 1 with resid.prior = fixed(1), because the augmented model has no free residual scale. And the leaf prior is stated with setCalibration, because a gaussian sampler built on a cold-start vector would otherwise inherit its prior scale from that vector’s range – an accident of the starting values, not a modelling choice.

set.seed(101L)
x <- matrix(runif(n * 3L), n, 3L)
fTrue <- 2 * (x[, 1L] - 0.5) + sin(2 * pi * x[, 2L])
o <- rep(0.25, n)
y <- rbinom(n, 1L, pnorm(fTrue + o))
control <- recipeControl(31L)

# the host: a gaussian sampler on the working response, sigma pinned at 1
host <- dbarts(x, 2 * y - 1 - o, control = control, resid.prior = fixed(1))
host$setCalibration(prior.scale = 2)

composed <- matrix(0, n, nDraws)
for (i in seq_len(nBurn + nDraws)) {
  # the fit WITHOUT the offset is what the augmentation conditions on; both
  # helpers form the linear predictor themselves as fit + offset
  z <- dbartsDrawLatents("probit", host$getFitsWithoutOffset(), y, offset = o)
  host$setResponse(dbartsWorkingResponse("probit", z, y, offset = o))
  host$run(0L, 1L)
  if (i > nBurn) composed[, i - nBurn] <- host$getFitsWithoutOffset()
}

# a native probit sampler, given the SAME leaf prior, targets the same posterior
native <- dbarts(x, y, offset = o, family = "probit", control = control,
                 node.prior = normal(k = 2, scale = 2))
nativeFit <- rowMeans(native$run(nBurn, nDraws)$train) - o
c(agreement = cor(rowMeans(composed), nativeFit),
  signal = cor(rowMeans(composed), fTrue))
## agreement    signal 
## 0.9928701 0.9222418

Agreement, not identity: these are two chains of one posterior, so they differ by Monte Carlo error. The package’s tests state the tolerance.

2. An outer block on the offset channel

The offset is the channel for anything additive that another block owns. Here the model is partially linear, yi=f(xi)+αwi+ϵiy_i = f(x_i) + \alpha w_i + \epsilon_i: BART holds ff, a conjugate normal block holds α\alpha, and each writes its own contribution into the other’s conditioning through setOffset.

The seeding contract is the whole of the correctness argument. The offset in force during a sweep must be the value the outer block currently holds, so the sampler is created with the initial offset installed and setOffset is called before run, never after. A sampler run once against a stale offset has drawn ff from the wrong conditional, and nothing later reports it.

alphaTrue <- 1.25
tau <- 2

set.seed(11L)
x <- matrix(runif(n * 3L), n, 3L)
w <- rnorm(n)
fTrue <- 3 * (x[, 1L] - 0.5)^2 + sin(2 * pi * x[, 2L])
y <- rnorm(n, fTrue + alphaTrue * w, 0.5)

alpha <- 0
control <- recipeControl(8L)
# created WITH the offset the loop's first sweep will run against
sampler <- dbarts(x, y, offset = alpha * w, control = control)

keepAlpha <- rep(NA_real_, nDraws)
for (i in seq_len(nBurn + nDraws)) {
  sampler$setOffset(alpha * w)              # install, then sweep
  sampler$run(0L, 1L)
  f <- as.numeric(sampler$getFitsWithoutOffset())
  sigma <- as.numeric(sampler$getSigmas())
  v <- 1 / (sum(w * w) / sigma^2 + 1 / tau^2)
  alpha <- rnorm(1L, v * sum(w * (y - f)) / sigma^2, sqrt(v))
  if (i > nBurn) keepAlpha[i - nBurn] <- alpha
}

c(mean = mean(keepAlpha), sd = sd(keepAlpha), truth = alphaTrue)
##       mean         sd      truth 
## 1.25913691 0.03649663 1.25000000

Checking the composition

Recovering the truth on one data set is not evidence that a sampler targets its posterior. dbartsValidateComposition runs simulation-based calibration over the same one-sweep step: it draws θ0\theta_0 from the prior, simulates data at it, starts the chain there, and ranks each functional’s value at θ0\theta_0 among the retained draws. Uniform ranks are what a correct kernel produces.

Stating the prior draw here means drawing ff from BART’s own prior, which sampleTreesFromPrior and sampleNodeParametersFromPrior do on the sampler itself. The problem is deliberately small, since every replication runs a full chain.

nSbc <- 60L
sigma0 <- 1
tauSbc <- 1

set.seed(4L)
xSbc <- matrix(runif(nSbc * 2L), nSbc, 2L)
wSbc <- rnorm(nSbc)
sbcControl <- dbartsControl(n.chains = 1L, n.threads = 1L, n.trees = 10L,
                            updateState = FALSE)

# the response the sampler is BUILT on fixes the response transform, and the
# leaf prior is then stated outright, so every replication shares one prior
newSampler <- function() {
  s <- dbarts(xSbc, seq(-3, 3, length.out = nSbc), control = sbcControl,
              resid.prior = fixed(sigma0^2))
  s$setCalibration(prior.scale = 2)
  s
}

drawPrior <- function() {
  s <- newSampler()
  s$sampleTreesFromPrior()
  s$sampleNodeParametersFromPrior()
  list(sampler = s, f = as.numeric(s$getFitsWithoutOffset()),
       alpha = rnorm(1L, 0, tauSbc))
}
simulateData <- function(theta0)
  rnorm(nSbc, theta0$f + theta0$alpha * wSbc, sigma0)
initState <- function(theta0, data) {
  theta0$sampler$setResponse(data)
  list(sampler = theta0$sampler, y = data, f = theta0$f, alpha = theta0$alpha)
}
step <- function(state) {
  state$sampler$setOffset(state$alpha * wSbc)
  state$sampler$run(0L, 1L)
  state$f <- as.numeric(state$sampler$getFitsWithoutOffset())
  v <- 1 / (sum(wSbc * wSbc) / sigma0^2 + 1 / tauSbc^2)
  state$alpha <- rnorm(1L, v * sum(wSbc * (state$y - state$f)) / sigma0^2,
                       sqrt(v))
  state
}
functionals <- function(state) c(alpha = state$alpha, f.mean = mean(state$f))

dbartsValidateComposition(drawPrior, simulateData, initState, step,
                          functionals, n.replications = 40L, n.draws = 50L,
                          n.thin = 5L, n.burn = 20L, seed = 12L)
## 
## Call:
## dbartsValidateComposition(drawPrior = drawPrior, simulate = simulateData, 
##     init = initState, step = step, functionals = functionals, 
##     n.replications = 40L, n.draws = 50L, n.thin = 5L, n.burn = 20L, 
##     seed = 12L)
## 
## 40 replications, 50 draws each (thin 5, burn 20)
## band alpha 0.05 over 2 functional(s) is 0.025; uniform mean rank 25.0
## 
##  functional mean.rank ecdf.diff  band chisq.p  ks.p verdict
##       alpha      24.6     0.109 0.223   0.395 0.664    PASS
##      f.mean      22.1     0.153 0.223   0.522 0.202    PASS

Reporting v * sum(wSbc * (state$y - state$f)) / sigma0^2 in place of the draw – the defect this diagnostic exists to catch – flags alpha here, and is a test cell of its own.

3. Several forests, one prior budget

An additive decomposition f(x)=∑k=1Kgk(x)f(x) = \sum_{k=1}^K g_k(x) over KK samplers is ordinary backfitting: each sampler regresses on the partial residual through setResponse. What does not come for free is the prior. Each sampler was built on the full response, so each carries a leaf prior sized for the whole of ff; their sum then has K\sqrt{K} times the prior standard deviation a single sampler would have, and nothing warns about it.

setCalibration(prior.scale = base / sqrt(K)) restates each forest’s share of one budget. The check below draws from the composed prior directly – sampleTreesFromPrior acts on the engine, so it sees what setCalibration wrote – and compares it with a single sampler’s.

K <- 2L

set.seed(21L)
x <- matrix(runif(n * 4L), n, 4L)
colnames(x) <- paste0("x", 1:4)
fTrue <- 2 * sin(pi * x[, 1L]) + x[, 2L] + 3 * (x[, 3L] - 0.5)^2 - 2 * x[, 4L]
y <- rnorm(n, fTrue, 0.5)

control <- recipeControl(5L)
blocks <- list(x[, 1:2, drop = FALSE], x[, 3:4, drop = FALSE])
samplers <- lapply(blocks, function(xb) dbarts(xb, y, control = control))

base <- samplers[[1L]]$getCalibration()[1L, "prior.scale"]
for (s in samplers) s$setCalibration(prior.scale = base / sqrt(K))

# the composed prior on the TOTAL, against a single sampler's
priorSd <- function(samplers) {
  draws <- replicate(200L, {
    total <- 0
    for (s in samplers) {
      s$sampleTreesFromPrior()
      s$sampleNodeParametersFromPrior()
      total <- total + as.numeric(s$getFitsWithoutOffset())
    }
    total
  })
  mean(apply(draws, 1L, sd))
}
single <- dbarts(x, y, control = control)
c(composed = priorSd(samplers), single = priorSd(list(single)))
## composed   single 
## 1.315185 1.411570
fits <- rep(list(rep(0, n)), K)
total <- matrix(0, n, nDraws)
for (i in seq_len(nBurn + nDraws)) {
  for (k in seq_len(K)) {
    samplers[[k]]$setResponse(y - Reduce(`+`, fits[-k]))
    samplers[[k]]$run(0L, 1L)
    fits[[k]] <- as.numeric(samplers[[k]]$getFitsWithoutOffset())
  }
  if (i > nBurn) total[, i - nBurn] <- Reduce(`+`, fits)
}
c(composed = cor(rowMeans(total), fTrue),
  single = cor(rowMeans(single$run(nBurn, nDraws)$train), fTrue))
##  composed    single 
## 0.9673282 0.9553002

setResponse leaves the response transform where creation put it (updateScale = FALSE, the default), which is what makes a per-sweep swap coherent: every sweep’s partial residual is read on one scale.

This is the case where every forest enters the response with a multiplier of one. vignette("gibbs_sampler_mixture_model", package = "dbarts") carries the general form, where forest ff enters through a known per-observation mf,im_{f,i}, along with its measured price and what it costs to reach the same posterior a forests = sampler targets.

4. A latent predictor shared by two samplers

When the quantity being sampled is a predictor rather than a response – a latent ability, a propensity, an unobserved dose – it moves through updatePredictorPerObservationJointly, which installs each observation in every sampler or in none. An observation is declined when its new value would empty a leaf in any tree of any sampler.

The returned mask is therefore part of the Metropolis accept decision, not a diagnostic. A declined observation was rolled back, so the log-likelihood read after the call is its old likelihood; treating the resulting ratio of 1 as an acceptance would move the host’s copy of the latent away from what the samplers actually hold, silently and permanently.

set.seed(404L)
nJ <- 80L
thetaTrue <- rnorm(nJ)
d1 <- data.frame(theta = thetaTrue, u = runif(nJ))
d1$y <- 1.5 * thetaTrue + rnorm(nJ, 0, 0.3)
d2 <- data.frame(v = runif(nJ), theta = thetaTrue)
d2$y <- rbinom(nJ, 1L, pnorm(thetaTrue))

control <- recipeControl(44L)
treePrior <- dbartsPriors$cgm(power = 0.5)
sA <- dbarts(y ~ theta + u, d1, control = control, tree.prior = treePrior)
sB <- dbarts(y ~ v + theta, d2, family = "probit", control = control,
             tree.prior = treePrior)
invisible(sA$run(0L, 20L))
invisible(sB$run(0L, 20L))

# per-observation log likelihood; with the trees held fixed, row i's fit is a
# function of row i's predictors alone, so this factorizes
logLik <- function() {
  fA <- as.numeric(sA$getFitsWithoutOffset())
  fB <- as.numeric(sB$getFitsWithoutOffset())
  dnorm(d1$y, fA, as.numeric(sA$getSigmas()), log = TRUE) +
    ifelse(d2$y == 1, pnorm(fB, log.p = TRUE), pnorm(-fB, log.p = TRUE))
}

current <- sA$data@x[, "theta"]
llCurrent <- logLik() + dnorm(current, 0, 1, log = TRUE)
proposal <- current + rnorm(nJ, 0, 0.5)

installed <- updatePredictorPerObservationJointly(list(sA, sB), proposal,
                                                  column = "theta")
llProposal <- logLik() + dnorm(proposal, 0, 1, log = TRUE)
# the conjunction: a declined observation is a REJECTED move
accept <- installed & (log(runif(nJ)) < llProposal - llCurrent)
theta <- ifelse(accept, proposal, current)
reinstalled <- updatePredictorPerObservationJointly(list(sA, sB), theta,
                                                    column = "theta")

c(installed = sum(installed), accepted = sum(accept),
  reinstalled = sum(reinstalled), n = nJ)
##   installed    accepted reinstalled           n 
##          77          40          80          80

The second call returns every observation to the value the host settled on. It reverts rows to values the samplers already held, so it is expected to be total; check its mask rather than assume it, since a FALSE there would mean the samplers and the host disagree about the current state.

5. An outer sampler that owns sigma

resid.prior = fixed(value) holds the residual variance at value and suppresses the sampler’s own draw, which is exactly what a host wants when sigma is drawn elsewhere – from a hierarchical prior, jointly with another outcome, or from a scale shared across several samplers. setSigma then writes it, and it stays written.

set.seed(505L)
x <- matrix(runif(n * 3L), n, 3L)
fTrue <- 2 * (x[, 1L] - 0.5) + sin(2 * pi * x[, 2L])
y <- rnorm(n, fTrue, 0.75)

sigma <- 1
control <- recipeControl(55L)
sampler <- dbarts(x, y, control = control, resid.prior = fixed(sigma^2))

keepSigma <- rep(NA_real_, nDraws)
for (i in seq_len(nBurn + nDraws)) {
  sampler$setSigma(sigma)                   # the sampler will not redraw it
  sampler$run(0L, 1L)
  f <- as.numeric(sampler$getFitsWithoutOffset())
  sigma <- sqrt(sum((y - f)^2) / rchisq(1L, n))
  if (i > nBurn) keepSigma[i - nBurn] <- sigma
}

c(mean = mean(keepSigma), truth = 0.75)
##      mean     truth 
## 0.6693388 0.7500000

The channel exists only where the model has a residual scale to own. A family that fixes it by definition refuses the write rather than accepting it and quietly rescaling every leaf posterior:

probit <- dbarts(x, rbinom(n, 1L, 0.5), family = "probit", control = control)
probit$setSigma(1)
## Error in `probit$setSigma()`:
## ! bartcore_setSigma: this response family fixes the residual standard deviation by definition; only gaussian and aft samplers carry a sigma to set

6. Reading the fit an incremental scheme needs

The last recipe is about a read, not a write. A host driving the sampler one sweep at a time conditions on f(xi)f(x_i), and $getFitsWithoutOffset() is the method that reports it. run()$train reports the same location with the installed offset folded in, and $getLatents() reports the augmentation variable, which carries no offset at all. Differencing the last two is the trap: getLatents() - run()$train is short by exactly the offset, so an outer block that regresses it on the offset’s own covariate recovers a coefficient shrunk toward zero.

gammaTrue <- 1.5

set.seed(314L)
x <- matrix(runif(n * 3L), n, 3L)
v <- rnorm(n)
fTrue <- 2 * (x[, 1L] - 0.5) + sin(2 * pi * x[, 2L])
y <- rbinom(n, 1L, pnorm(fTrue + gammaTrue * v))

gamma <- 0
control <- recipeControl(20L)
sampler <- dbarts(x, y, offset = gamma * v, family = "probit",
                  control = control)

keepGamma <- rep(NA_real_, nDraws)
for (i in seq_len(nBurn + nDraws)) {
  offset <- gamma * v
  sampler$setOffset(offset)
  train <- as.numeric(sampler$run(0L, 1L)$train)
  z <- as.numeric(sampler$getLatents())
  f <- as.numeric(sampler$getFitsWithoutOffset())
  # z - f, NOT z - train: the training channel carries the offset already
  vv <- 1 / (sum(v * v) + 1 / 4)
  gamma <- rnorm(1L, vv * sum(v * (z - f)), sqrt(vv))
  if (i > nBurn) keepGamma[i - nBurn] <- gamma
}

c(mean = mean(keepGamma), truth = gammaTrue,
  shortfall = max(abs((z - train) - ((z - f) - offset))))
##         mean        truth    shortfall 
## 1.371453e+00 1.500000e+00 4.440892e-16

The last column is zero by construction, which is the point: z - train and z - f differ by the installed offset exactly. Substituting train for f above pulls the posterior mean of γ\gamma from 1.37 to about 0.29, roughly seventeen oracle standard errors below the truth, on a run that reports no error at all.

7. A per-draw callback that never returns the array

Every recipe above drives a dbartsSampler from R, one sweep at a time. This one drives bart() itself and reads no returned fit back at all. callback fires a compiled function once per saved draw per chain, over const pointers into the engine’s own buffers, on the thread that owns that chain – so a reduction is taken as each draw is produced instead of over the n x S x C array bart() would otherwise build only to have the caller reduce it afterward. The shape is the one a compiled consumer wants: raw pointers and an opaque void* context, no SEXP crossing into the callback and nothing blocking on R. Rcpp is not a dependency of dbarts, so the code below does not run as part of building this vignette; ?bart’s callback and keepFits entries document the contract in full, and inst/tinytest/capi/consumer.c carries a plain-C copy of the same callback, checked against a fit’s own yhat.train.mean.

The task: a running posterior mean of the training fit, over x/y as in the recipes above, without ever holding the training draws at all.

Rcpp::sourceCpp("drawMean.cpp")     # makeMeanContext, meanCallbackPtr

nChains <- 4L
acc <- numeric(nrow(x) * nChains)   # the ONLY per-observation allocation
ctx <- makeMeanContext(acc, nrow(x), nChains)

fit <- bart(x, y, n.chains = nChains,
            callback = list(fn = meanCallbackPtr(), context = ctx))
means <- rowMeans(matrix(acc, nrow(x), nChains))
stopifnot(contextStatus(ctx) == 0L)
#include <Rcpp.h>
#include <dbarts/dbarts.h>   // dbarts_draw; PKG_CPPFLAGS -I the include dir

struct MeanContext {
  double* out;           // REAL() of the R vector, taken BEFORE the run
  std::size_t n, numChains;
  std::size_t* counts;   // per chain: no chain reads another's counter
  int status;            // set here, read from R after the run
};

extern "C" int meanCallback(void* context, const dbarts_draw* draw) {
  MeanContext* ctx = static_cast<MeanContext*>(context);
  if (draw->train == nullptr || draw->numObservations != ctx->n ||
      draw->numReportedLocations != 1 ||    // train is n x L; this reduces L = 1
      draw->chainIndex >= ctx->numChains) {
    ctx->status = 1;     // record and continue; nonzero would ABORT the run
    return 0;
  }
  double* out = ctx->out + draw->chainIndex * ctx->n;    // disjoint slice
  const double m = static_cast<double>(++ctx->counts[draw->chainIndex]);
  for (std::size_t i = 0; i < ctx->n; ++i)
    out[i] += (draw->train[i] - out[i]) / m;             // running mean
  return 0;
}

// freeMeanContext (not shown) deletes counts and the context

// [[Rcpp::export]]
SEXP meanCallbackPtr() {   // ...PtrFn: casting a function pointer to void* is
                           // what -Wpedantic flags under R CMD check
  return R_MakeExternalPtrFn(reinterpret_cast<DL_FUNC>(&meanCallback),
                             R_NilValue, R_NilValue);
}

// [[Rcpp::export]]
SEXP makeMeanContext(Rcpp::NumericVector acc, std::size_t n, std::size_t C) {
  MeanContext* ctx = new MeanContext{REAL(acc), n, C, new std::size_t[C](), 0};
  // acc goes in the PROTECTED slot (third argument): that is what keeps the
  // array alive as long as the context is
  SEXP ptr = PROTECT(R_MakeExternalPtr(ctx, R_NilValue, acc));
  R_RegisterCFinalizerEx(ptr, &freeMeanContext, TRUE);
  UNPROTECT(1);
  return ptr;
}

Four rules make this recipe correct rather than merely running, and every one is the caller’s to keep, not the engine’s. REAL(acc) is read exactly ONCE, before the fit starts: a later reassignment of acc in R builds a DIFFERENT vector, and the callback goes on writing the old one, so nothing between makeMeanContext and bart() may touch acc. Chains write DISJOINT slices – draw->chainIndex * ctx->n onward – which is what lets every chain’s calls run concurrently with no lock at all; two chains sharing a slice would need an atomic or a lock, giving up the bitwise reproducibility dbarts otherwise guarantees, for nothing this recipe needs. A context is built PER RUN, because drawIndex restarts at 0 on every bart() call (and every $run, for a dbartsSampler driven directly) – reusing one context across two fits overwrites the first fit’s slots rather than extending them. And the return value is an ABORT switch, not an error channel: nonzero stops the whole run at that draw and discards every chain’s results immediately, so a callback that merely disagrees with a draw’s shape – the if above – records a status and returns 0, leaving the caller to check contextStatus(ctx) (not shown; it reads ctx->status back) once the fit returns. Getting either of the last two wrong does not raise an R condition: it crashes the session outright, with nothing to tryCatch. Under all four sits the rule the header states in these terms: NO R API inside the callback, ever – not Rf_allocVector, not PROTECT, not Rf_error, and in C++ not the construction or destruction of an Rcpp proxy type, since Rcpp::NumericVector and its siblings touch R’s protection stack on both, allocation visible or not. R’s evaluator, allocator and protection stack belong to the main thread, and Rf_error would longjmp out of a context that thread established. That is the whole reason REAL(acc) is taken in makeMeanContext and only a raw double* crosses into meanCallback.

Supplying callback defaults keepFits to FALSE automatically, so this fit returns no yhat.train at all – means above, not a component of fit, is the only fitted value there is; passing keepFits = TRUE alongside callback keeps the array too, at the memory cost the callback exists to avoid. A strided variant that keeps every draw rather than reducing it on the fly is the same shape with a numDraws field added to MeanContext and the loop body replaced by one memcpy into out + (draw->chainIndex * numDraws + draw->drawIndex) * ctx->n.

Where to look next

?dbarts-embedding collects the channels, the reads and the rules the recipes above apply. ?dbartsSampler documents each method, including which quantity each reporting method returns; ?dbartsAugmentation documents the two augmentation helpers; ?dbartsValidateComposition documents the calibration check; and ?bart’s callback and keepFits entries document recipe 7’s contract, including the crash and lost-fitted-value warnings the recipe states in prose.
